summary: Specifies conventions for how S/MIME version 4.0 agents use X.509 certificates. Certificates are central to S/MIME processing, and agents validate them as described in RFC 5280. It is a standards-track document that goes with the S/MIME 4.0 message specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This document tells S/MIME mail programs what to do with the certificates that back a message's digital signature and encryption. It says which certificate and revocation list formats to accept, which signature algorithms to support, and how to check that the email address inside the certificate really belongs to the sender.

questions: which signature algorithms must s/mime support
how does s/mime check the sender email address
subtitle: The rules an S/MIME 4.0 mail agent must follow when it checks the certificates behind a message.

tldr.problem: S/MIME mail agents sign and encrypt messages using X.509 certificates, but the certificate rules of the PKIX profile alone do not say what a mail program must do with a certificate, a revocation list, or the email address inside it.
tldr.mechanism: The document states what agents must support: which certificate and revocation list formats to accept, which signature algorithms and key sizes to handle, which certificate extensions to obey, and how to check that the address in the certificate matches the sender of the message.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8550 replaces RFC 5750 as the certificate handling specification for S/MIME 4.0. It retires RSA with MD5, RSA and DSA with SHA-1, and DSA with SHA-256, and requires support for ECDSA with P-256 and for EdDSA with curve25519.

facts.label: Signature algorithms to support
facts.value: ECDSA with P-256 and SHA-256, EdDSA with curve25519

facts.label: RSA key size that MUST be supported

today: RFC 8550 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 5750 as the certificate handling specification for S/MIME 4.0, and the message format it works with is described in RFC 8551.

sections.title: What S/MIME Requires of Certificates
sections.content:
S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) version 4.0, described in RFC 8551, lets users send and receive secure MIME messages. Before a public key can be used to provide a security service, the S/MIME agent MUST verify that the key is valid. S/MIME agents MUST use PKIX certificates to validate public keys as described in RFC 5280, and they MUST also meet the certificate processing requirements in this document.

The document is compatible with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) defined in RFC 5652, because it uses the data types CMS defines, and it inherits the variety of certificate based key management architectures that CMS supports.

Version 4.0 agents ought to interoperate as widely as possible with agents for earlier versions. S/MIME version 2 is described in RFC 2311 through RFC 2315, version 3 in RFC 2630 through RFC 2634 and RFC 5035, version 3.1 in RFC 2634, RFC 3850, RFC 3851, RFC 3852 and RFC 5035, and version 3.2 in RFC 2634, RFC 5035, RFC 5652, RFC 5750 and RFC 5751.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a mail program uses a public key to sign or encrypt anything, it has to check that the key is genuine. This document says how S/MIME programs should do that, on top of the general rules for X.509 certificates.

sections.title: What Changed in S/MIME 4.0
sections.content:
The main change in version 4.0 is the set of cryptographic algorithms. Receiving agents MUST support ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) with P-256 and EdDSA (Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm) with curve25519. SHA-1 and MD5 are marked as historical because they are no longer considered secure, and DSA support is also historical because DSA has been replaced by elliptic curve versions. The lower bounds on RSA key sizes are increased.

Support for internationalized email addresses is now required. Appendix A collects the algorithms that earlier S/MIME versions asked for but that no longer meet modern security standards. Support of those algorithms may be needed to read historic S/MIME artifacts such as old messages or files, but they SHOULD NOT be used for new artifacts.

Appendix B moves the S/MIME version 2 certificate handling specification, RFC 2312, to Historic status, because the later versions are backward compatible with it except for the algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: Version 4.0 mainly changes which encryption and signing algorithms agents must handle. The old hash functions SHA-1 and MD5 are no longer accepted for new work, and two newer algorithms based on elliptic curves are now required.

sections.title: CMS Options and Certificate Choices
sections.content:
The CMS message format allows a wide variety of options in content and algorithm support. This section sets a base level of interoperability between all S/MIME implementations.

Receiving agents MUST support the CRL format defined in RFC 5280, including both version 1 and version 2 CRLs, and all agents MUST be able to perform revocation checks with CRLs and MUST perform revocation status checking in accordance with RFC 5280. Receiving agents MUST support v1 and v3 X.509 certificates, and SHOULD support X.509 version 2 attribute certificates (ACs).

Sending and receiving agents MUST NOT use PKCS #6 extended certificates, because the format is not in widespread use and PKIX certificate extensions cover the same ground. Receiving agents MUST be able to parse and process a message containing them, although ignoring them is expected. Sending agents MUST NOT send version 1 attribute certificates. Receiving agents MUST support chaining based on the distinguished name fields, and MUST handle an arbitrary number of certificates of arbitrary relationship to the sender and to each other in arbitrary order.
sections.plainLanguage: To make sure different mail programs can read each other's mail, the document fixes a small set of choices. Everyone must accept the standard revocation list format and the common certificate versions, and nobody should send the older PKCS #6 certificate format.

sections.title: Email Addresses in Distinguished Names
sections.content:
End-entity certificates MAY contain an Internet mail address. Addresses restricted to 7-bit ASCII use the pkcs-9-at-emailAddress object identifier and are encoded as described in Section 4.2.1.6 of RFC 5280. Internationalized addresses use the object identifier defined in RFC 8398. The address SHOULD be in the subjectAltName extension and SHOULD NOT be in the subject distinguished name.

Receiving agents MUST recognize and accept certificates that contain no email address, and MUST recognize both ASCII and internationalized addresses in the subjectAltName extension and in the distinguished name. The emailAddress attribute MUST be encoded as an IA5String and has an upper bound of 255 characters. For ASCII addresses the domain part, to the right of the '@', MUST be compared case-insensitively, and the local part SHOULD be compared case-insensitively as well.

Sending agents SHOULD make the address in the From or Sender header match an Internet mail address in the signer's certificate. Receiving agents MUST check that match when the certificate contains mail addresses, and SHOULD give the recipient some explicit alternate processing of the message, such as showing the addresses found in the certificate, if the comparison fails.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate can carry the email address of its owner. The receiving mail program has to compare that address with the From line of the message, and if they differ it should tell the user in some way rather than silently accept the message.

sections.title: Certificate Processing and Path Validation
sections.content:
Certificate, CRL and certification path validation MUST be performed as specified in RFC 5280 before a public key is used to verify a signature, to encrypt a content-encryption key, or to form a pairwise symmetric key. Certificates and CRLs reach the validation procedure from two places: incoming messages, and certificate and CRL retrieval mechanisms. Certificates in a message need not be in any particular order, and incoming certificates and CRLs SHOULD be cached for use in path validation.

Agents need a certificate retrieval mechanism. The document mentions an X.500 directory service as a retrieval-only mechanism, and RFC 8162, which describes an experimental protocol to retrieve certificates from the Domain Name System. At minimum, a user agent could generate a message to a recipient asking for the recipient's certificate in a signed reply. Receiving and sending agents SHOULD also provide a way to import and export certificates using a CMS certs-only message, so that whole chains can be moved rather than single certificates.

When verifying a signature, a signingCertificate attribute from RFC 2634 or a signingCertificateV2 attribute from RFC 5035 SHALL be used to identify the signer's certificate if one is present. Otherwise the certificate is identified either by its issuer name and serial number, or by its subject key identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking a certificate means building a chain from the signer's certificate up to a certificate authority the user already trusts, and checking at every step that nothing has been withdrawn. The certificates needed for that can come from the message itself or from a directory service.

sections.title: Signing Algorithms and Key Sizes
sections.content:
Certificates and CRLs are signed by the certificate issuer. Receiving agents MUST support ECDSA with curve P-256 with SHA-256, and MUST support EdDSA with curve25519 using PureEdDSA mode. They MUST- support RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 with SHA-256, where the MUST- level marks a requirement the authors expect to be dropped in a future document. They SHOULD support the RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS) with SHA-256.

Implementations SHOULD use deterministic generation for the parameter 'k' in ECDSA as outlined in RFC 6979, and EdDSA generates that parameter deterministically by definition.

For RSA and RSASSA-PSS key sizes, a key of 2047 bits or less SHOULD NOT be used, a key from 2048 to 4096 bits MUST be supported, and a key larger than 4096 bits MAY be supported. Curves other than P-256 and other curves than curve25519 MAY also be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a few signature algorithms are required. Two modern ones based on elliptic curves must work, and the older RSA method with SHA-256 is still expected but is on its way out. RSA keys must be at least 2048 bits to be accepted without complaint.

sections.title: PKIX Certificate Extensions
sections.content:
The basicConstraints extension delimits the role an issuing-authority or end-entity certificate plays in a certification path. Certificates MUST contain a basicConstraints extension in CA certificates and SHOULD NOT contain it in end-entity certificates.

The key usage extension limits the technical purposes for which a public key may be used. If it is present it MUST be marked as critical. Receiving agents MUST NOT accept the signature of a message that was verified with a certificate whose key usage extension lacks both the digitalSignature and the nonRepudiation bits. If the extension is absent, receiving clients MUST presume both bits are set.

The subject alternative name extension is the preferred way to convey the email addresses of the certificate holder. If the local part of the address is ASCII it MUST use the rfc822Name choice of the GeneralName type, and if it is not ASCII it MUST use the otherName choice as described in RFC 8398. The extended key usage extension also limits what a key may be used for, and the permitted uses are the intersection of the two extensions. An interpersonal-message receiving agent MUST check that the extended key usage extension contains either the id-kp-emailProtection object identifier or the anyExtendedKeyUsage object identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Four certificate extensions decide what a certificate may be used for. One says whether the holder is a certificate authority. One lists the allowed uses of the key, such as signing only. One carries the email addresses. One narrows the uses further, for example to email protection alone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All of the security issues faced by any cryptographic application must be faced by an S/MIME agent, including protecting the user's private key and helping the user avoid encrypting a message for the wrong recipient. If a certificate is not provably valid and associated with the message, the processing software should take immediate and noticeable steps to inform the end user.

Places where checking can fail include no mail address in the certificate matching the sender, no certificate chain leading to a trusted CA, no way to check the revocation list, an invalid or expired revocation list, an expired certificate, and a revoked certificate. When several unexpired revocation lists exist for a CA, an agent SHOULD consult the most recently issued one, because a sender could deliberately include an older list that does not mention a recent revocation.

Agents must also be careful about the time used for validity checks, since a signingTime attribute could be set to a time that lets an expired or revoked certificate pass. RSA keys of less than 2048 bits are now considered insecure by many experts and SHOULD no longer be used to sign certificates or CRLs. An implementation that supports verifying certificates or CRLs signed with RSA or DSA keys of less than 2048 bits MUST warn the user, and server implementations where user warnings are not appropriate SHOULD reject messages with weak cryptography.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking a certificate can fail in several ways, and the mail program must say so rather than quietly accept the message. It must also use the newest revocation list, use a trustworthy clock, and warn the user when it meets a certificate signed with a weak, short key.
